abstract: "Nonlinear, non-Gaussian partially observed Markov process (POMP) models arise in various areas including epidemiology, ecology, and robotics. Model-based inferences typically involve computationally intensive Monte Carlo methods.  We introduce Pypomp, a Python library for data analysis via POMP models that uses JAX to take advantage of GPU hardware, automatic differentiation, and just-in-time compilation. By design, Pypomp supports model development and data analysis as well as method development, following the approach of the pomp R package. However, Pypomp obtains considerably higher performance: Pypomp running on one GPU can obtain the throughput of 8,000 CPU cores running pomp. A central algorithm for Pypomp is the particle filter, and Pypomp is faster on our benchmark tests than other GPU-compatible particle filter libraries. The particle filter is differentiable, with a tunable bias-variance tradeoff."

```{python}
#| label: load-results
#| echo: false
# Benchmark results come from the pypomp/quant submodule (article/quant),
# and the England and Wales measles fit from ../big_measles. Every number
# quoted in the text is computed here, so rerunning quant updates the paper.
import json
import math
import subprocess
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pypomp as pp
from IPython.display import Markdown
from packaging.version import Version

QUANT = Path("quant")
TIMING_MODELS = {
    "dacca": "Cholera, Dhaka",
    "measles": "Measles, London",
    "panel_measles": "Measles, 4-town panel",
    "spx": "S\\&P 500",
}


def load_timing(model):
    """Timings and run metadata for one quant timing test, keyed by backend."""
    out = {}
    for backend in ["R", "cpu", "gpu", "gpu_jax"]:
        d = QUANT / "tests" / model / "timing" / "results" / backend
        if d.is_dir():
            out[backend] = {
                "times": pd.read_csv(d / "timings.csv").set_index("phase")["time_seconds"],
                "meta": json.loads((d / "latest.json").read_text()),
            }
    return out


def pf_time(times):
    # pypomp's cold-start time includes JIT compilation; R has no warm-up.
    return times.get("pfilter_cold", times.get("pfilter_warm"))


def latex_table(cols, head, body):
    """A table at the text width, as raw LaTeX for a tbl- div.

    Pandoc writes Markdown tables as longtables, which can break across pages
    and then repeat the caption. cols is the tabular column spec, head the
    header lines (with their own row ends), and body the rows without them.
    """
    lines = [
        "\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{4pt}",
        f"\\begin{{tabular*}}{{\\linewidth}}{{@{{\\extracolsep{{\\fill}}}}{cols}@{{}}}}",
        "\\toprule", *head, "\\midrule",
        *[row + " \\\\" for row in body],
        "\\bottomrule", "\\end{tabular*}",
    ]
    return Markdown("```{=latex}\n" + "\n".join(lines) + "\n```")


timing = {m: load_timing(m) for m in TIMING_MODELS}
quant_sha = subprocess.run(
    ["git", "-C", str(QUANT), "rev-parse", "--short", "HEAD"],
    capture_output=True, text=True, check=True,
).stdout.strip()
# The timing runs were not all made with the same Pypomp release.
_bench_versions = sorted(
    {r["meta"]["pypomp_version"] for t in timing.values() for b, r in t.items() if b != "R"},
    key=Version,  # handles release candidates such as 1.3.0rc1
)
pypomp_bench_version = (
    _bench_versions[0] if len(_bench_versions) == 1
    else f"{_bench_versions[0]}--{_bench_versions[-1]}"
)
pomp_bench_version = timing["dacca"]["R"]["meta"]["pomp_version"]
panelpomp_bench_version = timing["dacca"]["R"]["meta"]["panelPomp_version"]
r_bench_version = timing["dacca"]["R"]["meta"]["r_version"]
gpu_name = timing["dacca"]["gpu"]["meta"]["slurm"]["gpu_type"].replace("NVIDIA ", "")

# The R scripts run one doParallel worker per core on a 36-core node, and each
# phase splits independent searches or filters evenly across the workers, so
# one core would take R_CORES times as long. (latest.json's slurm.cpus is
# cpus-per-task, which is 1, not the number of workers.)
R_CORES = 36
mif_speedups = [
    t["R"]["times"]["mif"] / t["gpu"]["times"]["mif"] for t in timing.values()
]
mif_core_ratios = [R_CORES * s for s in mif_speedups]


def fmt_ratio(x):
    return f"{x:.1f}" if x < 10 else f"{x:.0f}"


# Split R time / GPU time into software (R / Pypomp on the same CPU node) and
# hardware (Pypomp CPU / Pypomp GPU), over the IF2 and PF rows of
# @tbl-timing-full that have a Pypomp CPU run.
software_ratios, hardware_ratios = [], []
for t in timing.values():
    if "cpu" in t:
        for get in [lambda s: s["mif"], pf_time]:
            r, py_cpu, gpu = (get(t[b]["times"]) for b in ["R", "cpu", "gpu"])
            software_ratios.append(r / py_cpu)
            hardware_ratios.append(py_cpu / gpu)

# GPU scaling tests: more chains at J = 1,000, or more particles per chain at a
# fixed number of chains. Each configuration ran in its own process with XLA
# preallocation off, so peak_vram_mb is the memory it actually used. IF2 ran
# twice with the same short M: the first run includes JIT compilation and the
# second does not. Project each configuration to the benchmark's IF2 length,
# compilation included, to compare with @tbl-timing.
def r_mif_config(model):
    """Particles per IF2 chain and IF2 iterations in the R timing run."""
    cfg = timing[model]["R"]["meta"]["run_config"]
    if model == "spx":
        return cfg["Np"], cfg["Nmif"]
    if model == "panel_measles":
        return cfg["NP_FITR"], cfg["NFITR"]
    return cfg["NP"], cfg["NFITR"]


def scaling_r_cores(model):
    s = pd.read_csv(QUANT / "tests" / model / "scaling/results/gpu/scaling.csv")
    np_r, nfitr = r_mif_config(model)
    # In the R timing run, each core ran one IF2 chain (over every unit of a panel).
    r_core_rate = np_r * nfitr / timing[model]["R"]["times"]["mif"]
    compile_s = s["mif_cold_seconds"] - s["mif_warm_seconds"]
    mif_s = compile_s + nfitr * s["mif_per_iter_seconds"]
    s["r_cores"] = s["total_particles_mif"] * nfitr / mif_s / r_core_rate
    return s


SCALING_MODELS = ["dacca", "measles", "panel_measles", "spx"]
scaling = {m: scaling_r_cores(m) for m in SCALING_MODELS}
peak_r_cores = {m: s["r_cores"].max() for m, s in scaling.items()}
peak_gain = {m: peak_r_cores[m] / c for m, c in zip(timing, mif_core_ratios)}


def bench_particles(model):
    """Total particles in flight during IF2 in the @tbl-timing benchmark."""
    cfg = timing[model]["R"]["meta"]["run_config"]
    return cfg.get("NSTARTS", cfg.get("Nstarts")) * r_mif_config(model)[0]


bench_totals = [bench_particles(m) for m in SCALING_MODELS]
peak_totals = [
    s.loc[s["r_cores"].idxmax(), "total_particles_mif"] for s in scaling.values()
]

spx_scaling = scaling["spx"]
spx_n_obs = len(pp.models.spx().ys)
n_dacca_obs = len(pp.models.dacca().ys)


# The two scaling branches were run on different grids of total particles, so
# compare them by interpolating each onto the range where they overlap.
def spx_throughput_at(kind, totals):
    s = spx_scaling[spx_scaling["scaling_type"] == kind].sort_values("total_particles_mif")
    return np.interp(np.log(totals), np.log(s["total_particles_mif"]), s["r_cores"])


spx_totals = spx_scaling.groupby("scaling_type")["total_particles_mif"]
spx_overlap = np.exp(np.linspace(
    np.log(spx_totals.min().max()), np.log(spx_totals.max().min()), 25
))
spx_chain_advantage = np.mean(
    spx_throughput_at("chains", spx_overlap) / spx_throughput_at("particles", spx_overlap)
)

# The configuration that used the most GPU memory across all scaling tests.
max_vram_model = max(scaling, key=lambda m: scaling[m]["peak_vram_mb"].max())
max_vram = scaling[max_vram_model].loc[scaling[max_vram_model]["peak_vram_mb"].idxmax()]

jax_sampler_slowdown = (
    timing["measles"]["gpu_jax"]["times"]["mif"] / timing["measles"]["gpu"]["times"]["mif"]
)
jax_sampler_pf_slowdown = (
    pf_time(timing["measles"]["gpu_jax"]["times"]) / pf_time(timing["measles"]["gpu"]["times"])
)
SAMPLERS = json.loads((QUANT / "tests/samplers/benchmark_results.json").read_text())
SAMPLER_ROWS = {  # distribution: label, cached regime with parameters across the switches
    "poisson": ("Poisson", "Mixed Rates (around switches)"),
    "binomial": ("Binomial", "Mixed Grid (around switches)"),
    "gamma": ("Gamma", "Mixed Shapes (around switch)"),
    "nbinomial": ("Negative binomial", "Mixed Grid (around switches)"),
}
max_w1_norm = max(max(g["w_dist_norm"]) for g in SAMPLERS["grids"].values())
# GPU speedup of pypomp.random over jax.random, for distributions jax.random has.
sampler_gpu_speedups = [
    t["t_jax_gpu"] / t["t_pp_gpu"]
    for t in (SAMPLERS[d][regime] for d, (_, regime) in SAMPLER_ROWS.items())
    if t.get("t_jax_gpu") is not None
]

# England and Wales measles fit (all 1,422 towns) on one GPU.
BIG = Path("../big_measles/results/2026-10-05_134449_u1422_L4_d001_reps36")
big_meta = json.loads((BIG / "metadata.json").read_text())
big_par = big_meta["parameters"]
# Wall-clock seconds for each method call. The total leaves out building the
# model and mixing and matching, which take about a minute together.
big_mif_s = big_par["stage_wall_s"]["mif"]
big_pf1_s = big_par["stage_wall_s"]["pfilter_eval1"]
big_pf2_s = big_par["stage_wall_s"]["pfilter_final"]
big_total_s = big_mif_s + big_pf1_s + big_pf2_s

# An earlier run with the same settings but a third as many searches.
BIG_SMALL = Path("../big_measles/results/2026-10-04_161213_u1422_L4_d001")
big_small_par = json.loads((BIG_SMALL / "metadata.json").read_text())["parameters"]
assert big_small_par["np_fitr"] == big_par["np_fitr"] and big_small_par["nfitr"] == big_par["nfitr"]
big_small_s = sum(big_small_par["stage_wall_s"][k] for k in ["mif", "pfilter_eval1", "pfilter_final"])
big_n_gpus = {2: "two", 3: "three", 4: "four"}[
    big_par["nreps_fitr"] // big_small_par["nreps_fitr"]
]

# R estimate, extrapolated from panelPomp's cost on the 4-town panel in quant,
# which covers the same 1950-1963 period with the same daily Euler steps. Cost
# is assumed linear in particles, IF2 iterations and towns. In the quant run,
# each of the 36 cores ran one IF2 chain and then NSTARTS * NREPS_EVAL / 36
# particle filters.
panel_R = timing["panel_measles"]["R"]
panel_cfg = panel_R["meta"]["run_config"]
n_small = len(panel_cfg["units"])
r_mif_cost = panel_R["times"]["mif"] / (panel_cfg["NP_FITR"] * panel_cfg["NFITR"] * n_small)
pf_per_core = panel_cfg["NSTARTS"] * panel_cfg["NREPS_EVAL"] / R_CORES
r_pf_cost = panel_R["times"]["pfilter_warm"] / (pf_per_core * panel_cfg["NP_EVAL"] * n_small)

n_big = big_par["n_units"]
# IF2 chains are sequential, so R gains nothing from more cores than chains.
r_big_mif_s = r_mif_cost * big_par["np_fitr"] * big_par["nfitr"] * n_big
r_one_pf_s = r_pf_cost * big_par["np_eval"] * n_big
r_big_pf1_s = math.ceil(big_par["nreps_fitr"] * big_par["nreps_eval"] / R_CORES) * r_one_pf_s
r_big_pf2_s = math.ceil(big_par["nreps_eval"] / R_CORES) * r_one_pf_s
r_big_total_s = r_big_mif_s + r_big_pf1_s + r_big_pf2_s
# On one core, every IF2 chain and particle filter runs in turn.
n_big_pf = big_par["nreps_fitr"] * big_par["nreps_eval"] + big_par["nreps_eval"]
r_big_1core_s = big_par["nreps_fitr"] * r_big_mif_s + n_big_pf * r_one_pf_s

# The particle filter workloads of @tbl-timing-full in other Python libraries
# (quant tests/library_comparison). first_s is the first call, including JIT
# compilation; status "timeout" means the run was stopped at first_s seconds,
# and "projected" means one CPU filter's time times the number of filters,
# divided by 36 cores. The pypomp column is release 1.2.0; pypomp_flat is the
# development version, which runs the replicates of a parameter set in parallel.
lib_times = pd.read_csv(QUANT / "tests/library_comparison/table.csv").set_index(["model", "column"])
lib_version = lib_times["version"].dropna().groupby(level="column").first()
GPU_LIBS = ["pfjax", "cuthbert", "pydpf"]
CPU_LIBS = ["particles", "pypfilt"]


def lib_s(model, lib):
    return lib_times.loc[(model, lib), "first_s"]


def lib_ratio(model, lib):
    """The other library's time divided by Pypomp's (release) time."""
    return lib_s(model, lib) / lib_s(model, "pypomp")


def lib_finished(model, lib):
    return lib_times.loc[(model, lib), "status"] != "timeout"


# jax.random-based libraries on the London measles model, relative to Pypomp.
lib_measles_jax = [lib_ratio("measles", l) for l in ["pfjax", "cuthbert"]]
lib_pydpf = [lib_ratio(m, "pydpf") for m in ["dacca", "measles", "panel_measles"]]
lib_dacca_jax = [lib_ratio("dacca", l) for l in ["pfjax", "cuthbert"]]
# The text names cuthbert as the fastest GPU library on the S&P 500 model.
assert min(GPU_LIBS, key=lambda l: lib_s("spx", l)) == "cuthbert"
assert all(lib_s("spx", "pypomp") > lib_s("spx", l) for l in GPU_LIBS)
assert all(lib_s("spx", "pypomp_flat") < lib_s("spx", l) for l in GPU_LIBS)
# CPU-only libraries relative to the measured pomp (or panelPomp) time.
lib_cpu_vs_r = {
    l: [lib_s(m, l) / pf_time(timing[m]["R"]["times"]) for m in TIMING_MODELS]
    for l in CPU_LIBS
}

HOUR, DAY = 3600, 86400
big_hours = f"{big_total_s / HOUR:.0f}"
big_small_hours = f"{big_small_s / HOUR:.0f}"
r_big_months = f"{r_big_total_s / (30.44 * DAY):.1f}"
big_speedup = f"{r_big_total_s / big_total_s:.0f}"
r_big_1core_years = f"{r_big_1core_s / (365.25 * DAY):.1f}"
big_core_ratio = f"{r_big_1core_s / big_total_s:,.0f}"
```

# Introduction {#sec-intro}
Partially observed Markov process (POMP) models provide a flexible framework for modeling dynamic systems whose underlying state is not directly observed.
POMP models are also known as state-space models or hidden Markov models.
<!--
, though these alternative names are sometimes restricted to continuous and discrete states respectively.
-->
Pypomp is a Python library combining advances in hardware, software, and algorithms for POMP models, with an emphasis on inference via the particle filter (PF).
PF, also known as sequential Monte Carlo, provides an estimate of the likelihood of a POMP model [@arulampalam02].
The basic PF algorithm needs to simulate from the process model but does not evaluate its transition probabilities, a property known as plug-and-play (P&P) [@breto09].
Pypomp focuses on P&P methods because they facilitate scientific modeling, enabling applications in epidemiology [@mietchen24; @fox22; @wen24], ecology [@augermethe21; @marino19; @blackwood13], finance [@breto14], robotics [@jonschkowski18] and other domains where nonlinear mechanistic stochastic dynamic models are pertinent.
Pypomp provides P&P inference methods extending PF: maximum likelihood parameter estimation by iterated filtering (IF2) [@ionides15], Bayesian inference by particle Markov chain Monte Carlo [@andrieu10], and stochastic gradient descent (SGD) via a differentiable particle filter (DPF) algorithm called a measurement-off-parameter (MOP) particle filter [@tan24].

Pypomp provides a framework for specifying models and inference methods, a range of pre-built models and methods, and various graphical and diagnostic tools to assist practical data analysis.
Thus, Pypomp supports complete data analysis workflows, facilitating the evaluation of a range of models and statistical methods.
Models and methods share an interface so that new models can readily be tested on pre-existing methods, and new methods can be tested on pre-existing models.
These design features are inherited from the R package pomp [@king16].
Although the method interface of Pypomp (and pomp) is not limited to P&P algorithms, experience has shown that P&P approaches are convenient for scientific data analysis.
Theoretical obstacles have limited the practical scope of non-P&P algorithms [@roberts01; @karppinen24].

Pypomp leverages JAX [@bradbury18] to provide just-in-time (JIT) compilation, automatic differentiation (AD), and capability to run on massively parallel hardware such as GPUs.
When the state space is small and discrete, or the model is linear Gaussian or close enough for effective approximation using Gaussian-inspired filters such as the extended Kalman filter, the particle filter is unnecessary, and the Dynamax library [@linderman25] provides JAX-based solutions.
Other JAX-based libraries providing PF and DPF methods for POMP models include PFJAX [@lysy22], Cuthbert [@duffield26] and pypfilt [@moss24].
PyDPF [@brady26] provides a DPF using Pytorch and focused on POMP models parameterized using neural networks.
The Python library particles [@chopin20] provides a general framework for sequential Monte Carlo computation without AD.
Pypomp distinguishes itself from these other packages by (i) following the design decisions of pomp that support a full data analysis workflow; (ii) superior performance on benchmark tests.
<!--
 in @tbl-timing.
-->
Pypomp is not limited to PF methods, for example, the approximate Bayesian computing (ABC) P&P algorithm of @marjoram03 has been implemented.
However, PF has proved an effective tool for the development and analysis of POMP models in scientific contexts.

With enough particles and method replications to saturate it, one GPU runs iterated filtering as fast as `{python} f"{min(peak_r_cores.values()):,.0f}"` to `{python} f"{max(peak_r_cores.values()):,.0f}"` CPU cores running pomp (Appendix -@sec-scaling).
Such replications are routine in practice: practical likelihood maximization involves searching from many initial parameter vectors, and Monte Carlo adjusted profile (MCAP) confidence intervals [@ionides17], implemented in Pypomp as `mcap`, require maximizations.
Profile likelihood have been found preferable to Fisher information for confidence interval construction for linear Gaussian POMP models [@wheeler25arma].
For Monte Carlo methods, MCAP algorithms can lead to efficient inference even in a limit where the Monte Carlo error grows as the amount of data increases [@ning21].
<!--
GPU hardware makes P&P likelihood-based inference feasible at previously intractable scales: one GPU fits a panel POMP model to the England and Wales measles data of @korevaar20, over one million observations from `{python} f"{n_big:,}"` towns and cities, in `{python} big_hours` hours, compared with an estimated `{python} r_big_months` months for panelPomp on a 36-core node (@sec-performance).
-->

Algorithms to take advantage of JIT, AD, and GPU are an area of active development.
Pypomp implements the MOP P&P DPF algorithm of @tan24, with the resulting derivative being called DMOP and implemented as the `dmop` method.
DMOP is competitive on benchmark problems when combined with Adam SGD, especially when using IF2 for a warm start [@tan24].
Pypomp provides inverse transform sampling methods for use in `rproc` and `rmeas` since the rejection sampling used in some `jax.random` samplers is inefficient on GPUs [@giles16; @giles24; @temme92].
These Pypomp samplers run `{python} f"{min(sampler_gpu_speedups):.0f}"` to `{python} f"{max(sampler_gpu_speedups):.0f}"` times faster than their `jax.random` counterparts on a GPU.
Quantiles of draws from inverse sampling and rejection sampling differ by at most `{python} f"{max_w1_norm * 100:.1f}"`% of a standard deviation on average (Appendix -@sec-samplers).

# POMP Modeling in Pypomp {#sec-pomp}

A POMP model consists of an unobserved Markov process $\{X(t), t_0 \leq t \leq t_{N}\}$ and observable $Y_{1:N}$ at times $t_{1:N}$ with observed value $y^*_{1:N}$.
The initial state is $X(t_0)$, $X_n := X(t_n)$, and $Y_n$ is independent of $Y_m, X_m$, $m \neq n$, conditional on $X_n$.
P&P methods need only a simulator for the initial state, $X_0 \sim f_{X_0}(x_0 ; \theta)$, a simulator for the state transition, $X_{n+1} \sim f_{X_{n+1}|X_{n}}(x_{n+1} | x_{n} ; \theta)$, and the measurement density $f_{Y_n|X_n}(y_n| x_n; \theta)$, where $\theta$ denotes the model parameters. 
The user passes data and JAX-compatible code for these functions to build a `Pomp` class model object using the `Pomp` consctructor function.
For P&P methods, it suffices to specify an initial value for the latent dynamic system (known as `rinit`), a latent process simulator (`rproc`), a measurement density simulator (`rmeas`) and a measurement density evaluator (`dmeas`).
Tutorials are available at [https://github.com/pypomp/tutorials](https://github.com/pypomp/tutorials).
Models included in Pypomp include a model for historical monthly cholera mortality in Dhaka, Bangladesh (`pypomp.models.dacca`), historical weekly measles cases in London, UK (`pypomp.models.measles.pomp`), daily closing price for the S&P 500 index (`pypomp.models.spx`), and a panel model for measles cases in up to 1422 urban and rural districts in England and Wales (`pypomp.models.measles.panel_pomp`).

Below, we demonstrate maximum likelihood estimation with IF2 (`mif`) followed by refinement using SGD (`train`) and then log-likelihood evaluation using PF (`pfilter`), on the `spx` model.
Each method stores its convergence records, execution time, and arguments in the `results_history` attribute of the `Pomp` object, enabling sequential method chaining and diagnostic investigation by helper methods such as `traces`. 
```{python}
# | label: spx-inference-workflow
# | echo: true
# | cache: true
import pypomp as pp, jax
spx_obj = pp.models.spx()
spx_obj.mif(J=1000, M=10, key=jax.random.key(1),
    rw_sd = pp.RWSigma( 
        sigmas={"mu": 0.02, "kappa": 0.02, "theta": 0.02, 
            "xi": 0.02, "rho": 0.02, "V_0": 0.1}, 
        init_names=["V_0"],
    ).geometric_cooling(a=0.5)) 
spx_obj.train(J=1000, M=10, optimizer=pp.Adam(),
    eta = pp.LearningRate(
        {name: 0.001 for name in spx_obj.canonical_param_names}
    ).geometric_decay(decay_rate=0.5, M=10)) 
spx_obj.pfilter(J=1000, reps=10) 
```

A collection of POMP models is a PanelPOMP [@breto20], and each constituent POMP is called a _unit_.
Parameters may be unit-specific or shared between units.
Marginalized panel iterated filtering (MPIF) [@wheeler25] and DMOP provide likelihood maximization for models of class `PanelPomp`.

# Performance {#sec-performance}

Two performance questions are: (i) what is the benefit of using GPU hardware versus CPU? (ii) how does Pypomp compare in speed to altnernative GPU-based particle filter libraries? 
To address (i), we compare Pypomp on a GPU with pomp on a CPU because that informs a natural decision for scientists considering Pypomp as a data analysis tool. 
Model code in pomp is usually written via compiled snippets of C code, and so pomp has comparable speed to other high-performance CPU-based packages for POMP models [@fitzjohn20]. 
Results are shown in @tbl-timing on four models with different characteristics. 
Additional details are in Appendix -@sec-benchmarks and <https://github.com/pypomp/quant>.
Relative efficiency varies with the number of particles, with the highest efficiency occurring when the GPU cores are saturated (Appendix -@sec-scaling).
The GPU times for the measles models use the GPU-adapted samplers in `pypomp.random`: with standard algorithms, such as `jax.random` samplers, IF2 for the London measles model took `{python} f"{jax_sampler_slowdown:.0f}"` times longer (Appendix -@sec-samplers).
To address (ii), Appendix -@sec-libraries runs the same particle filter workloads in five other Python libraries.
On the London measles model, `pfjax` and `cuthbert` took `{python} f"{min(lib_measles_jax):.0f}"` to `{python} f"{max(lib_measles_jax):.0f}"` times as long as Pypomp on a GPU.

::: {#tbl-timing}
```{python}

latex_table(

        " & \\texttt{pomp} & Pypomp & & CPU cores & Peak cores \\\\",
```

# Full benchmark results {#sec-benchmarks}

The four benchmark models stress different parts of the particle filter, which helps locate performance bottlenecks.

**Cholera, Dhaka.**
The cholera model of @king08 has `{python} f"{n_dacca_obs:,}"` monthly observations with 20 Euler steps between each, and each step updates a stochastic differential equation with one normal draw.
The process model is cheap, but there are many steps between resamples, so this model isolates the per-step overhead inside the process model.

**Measles, London.**
The measles model of @he10 has weekly case reports from 1950 to 1963 and takes a daily Euler step, interpolating covariates and drawing binomial, gamma, and Poisson random variables at every step.
It has a relatively expensive process model, so it isolates how the GPU handles heavy computation per particle, whilte testing the fast samplers in `pypomp.random` (Appendix -@sec-samplers).

**Measles, 4-town panel.**
The panel model fits the same measles model to `{python} ", ".join(panel_cfg["units"][:-1])`, and `{python} panel_cfg["units"][-1]` jointly, with some parameters shared across towns and the rest specific to each town.
MPIF [@wheeler25] filters the towns sequentially within each iteration, so an iteration costs about four single-town iterations with the same number of particles in flight.
This model tests the panel methods used in Appendix -@sec-big-measles-details.
Its ratio of R pomp CPU time to GPU time is lower than for the London model because R runs it relatively fast, likely because the random variate generators in R can take a cheaper route for the smaller parameter values of the smaller towns.

**S&P 500.**
The stochastic volatility model of @breto14 has `{python} f"{spx_n_obs:,}"` daily log returns and takes one step of its process model per observation, with a single normal draw.
Each step between resamples is very cheap, so fixed per-observation costs such as resampling can dominate.

```{python}
#| echo: false

def bench_workload(model):
    """IF2 particles, iterations, and searches, and PF replicates per parameter set.

    The quant scripts name these settings differently for each model and
    language, so read them from every backend's run and check that they agree.
    """
    workloads = set()
    for run in timing[model].values():
        cfg = {k.upper(): v for k, v in run["meta"]["run_config"].items()}
        np_fitr = cfg.get("NP_FITR", cfg.get("NP"))
        # Every benchmark filters with as many particles as IF2 uses.
        assert cfg.get("NP_EVAL", np_fitr) == np_fitr, model
        workloads.add((
            np_fitr,
            cfg.get("NFITR", cfg.get("NMIF")),
            cfg["NSTARTS"],
            cfg.get("NREPS_EVAL", cfg.get("NREPS")),
        ))
    assert len(workloads) == 1, (model, workloads)
    return workloads.pop()


workload = {m: bench_workload(m) for m in TIMING_MODELS}
# The text below describes the cholera and both measles benchmarks together.
assert workload["dacca"] == workload["measles"] == workload["panel_measles"], workload
assert workload["spx"][2] == workload["dacca"][2], workload
wl_np, wl_nfitr, wl_nstarts, wl_nreps = workload["dacca"]
spx_np, spx_nfitr, _, spx_nreps = workload["spx"]
```

@tbl-timing benchmarks Pypomp `{python} pypomp_bench_version` against pomp `{python} pomp_bench_version` and panelPomp `{python} panelpomp_bench_version`.
R pomp and Pypomp run the same workload in a given benchmark.
Each benchmark runs `{python} wl_nstarts` IF2 searches from the same starting points and then runs replicate particle filters at each search's IF2 estimate, with as many particles per filter as per search.
The cholera and both measles benchmarks use `{python} f"{wl_np:,}"` particles, `{python} wl_nfitr` IF2 iterations, and `{python} wl_nreps` particle filter replicates, and the S&P 500 benchmark uses `{python} f"{spx_np:,}"` particles, `{python} spx_nfitr` iterations, and `{python} spx_nreps` replicates.

Fitting the measles model of @he10 to all `{python} f"{n_big:,}"` towns and cities for 1950--1963 took one GPU `{python} big_hours` hours, including likelihood evaluation, versus an estimated `{python} r_big_months` months for R on a 36-core node, extrapolating linearly from panelPomp's cost on the 4-town panel (Appendix -@sec-big-measles-details).
Thus, Pypomp enables a scientific analysis that was previously considered unfeasible [@becker17].

@tbl-timing-full extends @tbl-timing with particle filter times for Pypomp on CPU, using the same 36 cores used for R pomp.
Pypomp on CPU was `{python} fmt_ratio(min(software_ratios))` to `{python} fmt_ratio(max(software_ratios))` times faster than R pomp, and moving Pypomp to the GPU makes it another `{python} fmt_ratio(min(hardware_ratios))` to `{python} fmt_ratio(max(hardware_ratios))` times faster.
These workloads are sized for R and too small to saturate the GPU, so the hardware and total ratios understate what the GPU can do.
At its peak throughput in the scaling tests (Appendix -@sec-scaling), one GPU runs IF2 `{python} f"{min(peak_r_cores.values()) / R_CORES:.0f}"` to `{python} f"{max(peak_r_cores.values()) / R_CORES:.0f}"` times as fast as R on the 36-core node.

::: {#tbl-timing-full}
```{python}
#| echo: false

def fmt_s(x):
    if x is None or pd.isna(x):
        return "---"
    return f"{x:,.0f}" if x >= 100 else f"{x:.1f}"


def fmt_x(x):
    return "---" if x is None else fmt_ratio(x) + "$\\times$"


rows = []
for model, label in TIMING_MODELS.items():
    t = timing[model]
    cpu = t.get("cpu", {}).get("times")
    for task, get in [("IF2", lambda s: s["mif"]), ("PF", pf_time)]:
        r, gpu = get(t["R"]["times"]), get(t["gpu"]["times"])
        py_cpu = None if cpu is None else get(cpu)
        software = r / py_cpu if py_cpu is not None else None
        hardware = py_cpu / gpu if py_cpu is not None else None
        rows.append(
            f"{label if task == 'IF2' else ''} & {task} & {fmt_s(r)} "
            f"& {fmt_s(py_cpu)} & {fmt_s(gpu)} & {fmt_x(software)} "
            f"& {fmt_x(hardware)} & {fmt_x(r / gpu)}"
        )
latex_table(
    "llrrrrrr",
    [
        " & & \\texttt{pomp} & \\multicolumn{2}{c}{Pypomp} & \\multicolumn{3}{c}{Ratio} \\\\",
        "\\cmidrule(lr){4-5} \\cmidrule(lr){6-8}",
        "Model & Task & 36 cores & 36 cores & 1 GPU & Software & Hardware & Total \\\\",

```

Wall-clock time in seconds for IF2 and for particle filter (PF) evaluation, with the workloads described above. Pypomp IF2 and PF times include JIT compilation. Software ratio is the pomp (or panelPomp) time divided by the Pypomp time on the same 36 cores, hardware ratio is the Pypomp CPU time divided by the Pypomp GPU time, and total is their product, the pomp time divided by the Pypomp GPU time. These workloads do not saturate the GPU, so the hardware and total ratios understate its throughput; peak cores matched in @tbl-timing gives the GPU's highest measured IF2 throughput. The 4-town panel has no Pypomp CPU run.

# Comparison with other particle filter libraries {#sec-libraries}

@tbl-libraries times the particle filter workloads of @tbl-timing-full in other Python particle filter libraries, with each model written as a user of that library would write it.
Every library runs the bootstrap particle filter with the same number of filters and particles as in @tbl-timing-full.
The GPU libraries ran on one RTX 3090, a slower GPU than the one used in @tbl-timing, and with a different Pypomp release, so the Pypomp times in @tbl-libraries are not comparable with those in @tbl-timing-full.
We left out Dynamax [@linderman25], since its only particle filter is a Rao--Blackwellized filter for switching linear Gaussian models.

On the cholera model, `pfjax` and `cuthbert` took `{python} f"{min(lib_dacca_jax):.1f}"` to `{python} f"{max(lib_dacca_jax):.1f}"` times as long as Pypomp, so the three JAX libraries performed about the same.
On the measles models, `pfjax` and `cuthbert` were `{python} f"{min(lib_measles_jax):.0f}"` to `{python} f"{max(lib_measles_jax):.0f}"` times slower than Pypomp for London, and neither finished the 4-town panel within an hour.
Most of this gap comes from the `jax.random` rejection samplers, which these libraries use for the binomial, gamma, and Poisson draws of the measles model (Appendix -@sec-samplers).
The PyTorch library `pydpf` took `{python} f"{min(lib_pydpf):.1f}"` to `{python} f"{max(lib_pydpf):.1f}"` times as long as Pypomp on the cholera and measles models.

The S&P 500 model is the exception.
Its steps are cheap, so the cost of running each parameter set's replicate filters one after another dominates, and Pypomp `{python} lib_version["pypomp"]` was the slowest of the GPU libraries, taking `{python} f"{lib_s('spx', 'pypomp'):.1f}"` seconds against `{python} f"{lib_s('spx', 'cuthbert'):.1f}"` seconds for `cuthbert`.
The development version of Pypomp runs these replicates in parallel and takes `{python} f"{lib_s('spx', 'pypomp_flat'):.1f}"` seconds, faster than every other GPU library.

The CPU-only libraries `particles` and `pypfilt` were timed on one core, and we scaled each time to 36 cores assuming perfect scaling, which flatters them.
Under this assumption, `particles` took `{python} f"{min(lib_cpu_vs_r['particles']):.1f}"` to `{python} f"{max(lib_cpu_vs_r['particles']):.1f}"` times the measured pomp time, and `pypfilt` took `{python} f"{min(lib_cpu_vs_r['pypfilt']):.1f}"` to `{python} f"{max(lib_cpu_vs_r['pypfilt']):.1f}"` times the pomp time.

::: {#tbl-libraries}

# GPU scaling tests {#sec-scaling}

```{python}
#| label: scaling-plot-setup
#| echo: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.ticker import FuncFormatter, NullFormatter
from matplotlib_inline.backend_inline import set_matplotlib_formats

set_matplotlib_formats("pdf")  # vector output for the PDF manuscript

# Categorical slots 1 and 2 of the dataviz reference palette (validated for
# color-vision deficiency); marker shape is a second cue for grayscale print.
BLUE, ORANGE = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834"
INK, MUTED, GRID = "#222222", "#6b6b6b", "#e4e4e0"
plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.size": 8, "axes.edgecolor": MUTED, "axes.labelcolor": INK,
    "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "axes.linewidth": 0.6,
})


def log_axis(axis, ticks, lo, hi):
    """Log scale with plain-number labels at the given ticks between lo and hi."""
    axis.axes.set_xscale("log") if axis is axis.axes.xaxis else axis.axes.set_yscale("log")
    axis.set_ticks([t for t in ticks if lo <= t <= hi])
    axis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:,g}"))
    axis.set_minor_formatter(NullFormatter())
    (axis.axes.set_xlim if axis is axis.axes.xaxis else axis.axes.set_ylim)(lo, hi)


def bench_point(model):
    """Total IF2 particles (millions) and R cores matched in the @tbl-timing benchmark."""
    cores = R_CORES * timing[model]["R"]["times"]["mif"] / timing[model]["gpu"]["times"]["mif"]
    return bench_particles(model) / 1e6, cores


SCALING_TITLES = {
    "dacca": "Cholera, Dhaka",
    "measles": "Measles, London",
    "panel_measles": "Measles, 4-town panel",
    "spx": "S&P 500",
}


def plot_scaling():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.5, 4.2), constrained_layout=True)
    for ax, model in zip(axes.flat, SCALING_MODELS):
        s = scaling[model]
        millions = s["total_particles_mif"] / 1e6
        for kind, label, color, marker in [
            ("chains", "More searches, 1,000 particles each", BLUE, "o"),
            ("particles", "More particles, fixed number of searches", ORANGE, "s"),
        ]:
            k = s["scaling_type"] == kind
            ax.plot(millions[k], s.loc[k, "r_cores"], color=color, marker=marker,
                    markersize=3.5, linewidth=1.3, label=label)
        bench_x, bench_y = bench_point(model)
        ax.plot(bench_x, bench_y, marker="D", markersize=4, color=INK,
                linestyle="none", label="Benchmark (Table 1)")
        log_axis(ax.xaxis, [0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3],
                 min(millions.min(), bench_x) / 1.3, millions.max() * 1.3)
        ax.set_ylim(0, max(s["r_cores"].max(), bench_y) * 1.1)
        ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda y, _: f"{y:,.0f}"))
        ax.set_title(SCALING_TITLES[model], fontsize=8, color=INK, loc="left")
        ax.grid(True, color=GRID, linewidth=0.6)
        ax.set_axisbelow(True)
        for side in ("top", "right"):
            ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
    for ax in axes[1]:
        ax.set_xlabel("Total particles (millions)")
    for ax in axes[:, 0]:
        ax.set_ylabel("R cores matched")
    handles, labels = axes[0, 0].get_legend_handles_labels()
    fig.legend(handles, labels, loc="outside upper center", ncol=3, frameon=False)
    plt.show()


def best(model):
    return scaling[model].loc[scaling[model]["r_cores"].idxmax()]


scaling_m = sorted({int(s["M"].iloc[0]) for s in scaling.values()})
fixed_chains = sorted({
    int(s.loc[s["scaling_type"] == "particles", "chains"].iloc[0]) for s in scaling.values()
})
```

The benchmarks in @tbl-timing and @tbl-timing-full use the R configuration, which does not give the GPU enough work to reach its highest throughput for every model.
The scaling tests in quant ran IF2 on one `{python} gpu_name` GPU with more particles in flight, added in two ways: more searches of 1,000 particles each, or more particles for each of a fixed number of searches.
Each configuration ran in its own process and ran a short IF2 twice, so that the second run excludes JIT compilation.
We project each configuration's time to the benchmark's number of IF2 iterations, including compilation, and divide the benchmark's R time by it to get the number of CPU cores running R that one GPU matches.
This assumes that R's time grows linearly with the number of particles and searches.
The highest of these values is the Peak column of @tbl-timing.
JAX's memory preallocation was turned off, so the peak GPU memory is the memory each configuration used.
No scaling test used more than `{python} f"{max_vram['peak_vram_mb'] / 1024:.1f}"` GB of GPU memory, the peak for the cholera model with `{python} f"{max_vram['total_particles_mif'] / 1e6:.1f}"` million particles.

@fig-scaling shows the results.
For every model, throughput peaks at between `{python} f"{min(best(m)['total_particles_mif'] for m in scaling) / 1e6:.1f}"` and `{python} f"{max(best(m)['total_particles_mif'] for m in scaling) / 1e6:.1f}"` million particles and falls or plateaus at larger sizes.
The peak is `{python} f"{peak_gain['dacca']:.1f}"` times the benchmark for the cholera model, `{python} f"{peak_gain['measles']:.1f}"` times for the London measles model, `{python} f"{peak_gain['panel_measles']:.1f}"` times for the 4-town panel, and `{python} f"{peak_gain['spx']:.1f}"` times for the S&P 500 model.
The S&P 500 model gains the most because its benchmark, with cheap steps and few particles, leaves the GPU mostly idle.
For this model, adding searches beats adding particles per search at a given total number of particles by an average of `{python} f"{(spx_chain_advantage - 1) * 100:.0f}"`%.
Consequently, there is not a large difference in speed between adding searches or particles per search on the GPU in terms of scaling with total particles.

::: {#fig-scaling}

IF2 throughput on one GPU, as the number of CPU cores running R that the GPU matches, against the total number of particles in flight. Blue adds searches of 1,000 particles each; orange adds particles to each of `{python} " or ".join(map(str, fixed_chains))` searches. Each configuration ran `{python} " or ".join(map(str, scaling_m))` IF2 iterations, projected to the benchmark's number. The x-axes use a log scale.

# Random variable samplers {#sec-samplers}

`jax.random` draws Poisson, binomial, and gamma random variables with rejection samplers, which loop a random number of times per draw.
This suits GPUs poorly, since threads that run together wait for the slowest one.
`pypomp.random` instead provides approximate inverse-CDF samplers, which avoid rejection loops.
@tbl-samplers compares the two on 1,000,000 draws per call, with parameters spread across the values where each sampler switches algorithms, averaged over 20 calls.
The approximation error is small: over a grid of parameter values, the Wasserstein distance between 1,000,000 draws from each `pypomp.random` sampler and from a reference sampler is at most `{python} f"{max_w1_norm * 100:.1f}"`% of the reference standard deviation.
In the London measles benchmark, the `jax.random` samplers made IF2 `{python} f"{jax_sampler_slowdown:.0f}"` times slower and particle filtering `{python} f"{jax_sampler_pf_slowdown:.0f}"` times slower on the GPU.

::: {#tbl-samplers}
```{python}
#| echo: false
def fmt_ms(x):
    return "---" if x is None else (f"{x:,.0f}" if x >= 100 else f"{x:.2f}")


def ratio(num, den):
    return "---" if num is None else f"{num / den:.0f}$\\times$"


rows = []
for dist, (label, regime) in SAMPLER_ROWS.items():
    t = SAMPLERS[dist][regime]
    jax_gpu, jax_cpu = t.get("t_jax_gpu"), t.get("t_jax_cpu")
    w1 = max(SAMPLERS["grids"][dist]["w_dist_norm"])
    rows.append(
        f"{label} & {fmt_ms(t['t_pp_gpu'])} & {fmt_ms(jax_gpu)} & {ratio(jax_gpu, t['t_pp_gpu'])} "
        f"& {fmt_ms(t['t_pp_cpu'])} & {fmt_ms(jax_cpu)} & {ratio(jax_cpu, t['t_pp_cpu'])} & {w1:.3f}"
    )
latex_table(
    "lrrrrrrr",
    [
        "& \\multicolumn{3}{c}{GPU} & \\multicolumn{3}{c}{CPU} & \\\\",
        "\\cmidrule(lr){2-4} \\cmidrule(lr){5-7}",
        "Distribution & \\texttt{pypomp} & \\texttt{jax} & Ratio "
        "& \\texttt{pypomp} & \\texttt{jax} & Ratio & Max $W_1/\\sigma$ \\\\",
    ],
    rows,
)
```

Time in milliseconds for 1,000,000 draws from `pypomp.random` and `jax.random`, on one GPU and on one CPU core, with parameters spread across the values where the samplers switch algorithms. Ratio is the `jax.random` time divided by the `pypomp.random` time. `jax.random` has no negative binomial sampler. Max $W_1/\sigma$ is the largest Wasserstein distance between `pypomp.random` draws and draws from `jax.random` (or `scipy.stats` for the negative binomial) over a grid of parameter values, relative to the standard deviation.
:::

# England and Wales measles fit {#sec-big-measles-details}

We ran `{python} big_par["nreps_fitr"]` MPIF searches, each with `{python} f"{big_par['np_fitr']:,}"` particles for `{python} big_par["nfitr"]` iterations, and evaluated each endpoint with `{python} big_par["nreps_eval"]` particle filter replicates of `{python} f"{big_par['np_eval']:,}"` particles.
We then combined the best estimate for each town across searches and evaluated the result with another `{python} big_par["nreps_eval"]` replicates.
@tbl-big-measles gives the time for each stage on one GPU with Pypomp `{python} big_meta["environment"]["pypomp_version"]`.

For comparison, we estimated how long the same computation would take with panelPomp on a 36-core CPU node.
We measured panelPomp's cost per particle, per IF2 iteration, and per town on the 4-town panel in @tbl-timing-full, which covers the same period with the same daily time step, and scaled it linearly to the full computation.
We assume panelPomp fits the towns jointly with MPIF, as Pypomp did, so each search runs on one core and does not parallelize across units -- this would be necessary in the general case when using shared parameters.
By this estimate, R would need about `{python} r_big_months` months, `{python} big_speedup` times longer than the GPU, and about `{python} r_big_1core_years` years on a single core, so the GPU delivered the throughput of about `{python} big_core_ratio` CPU cores running R.
The wall clock time can be reduced further by spreading the replication over multiple GPUs; for example, a run with the same settings but only `{python} big_small_par["nreps_fitr"]` searches took one GPU `{python} big_small_hours` hours, so `{python} big_n_gpus` GPUs running `{python} big_small_par["nreps_fitr"]` searches each would finish in about `{python} big_small_hours` hours instead of `{python} big_hours`.

::: {#tbl-big-measles}
```{python}
#| echo: false


def fmt_dur(s):
    if s >= 2 * DAY:
        return f"{s / DAY:.1f} days"
    if s >= 2 * HOUR:
        return f"{s / HOUR:.1f} hours"
    return f"{s / 60:.0f} minutes"


stages = [
    ("IF2", big_mif_s, r_big_mif_s),
    ("PF, all search endpoints", big_pf1_s, r_big_pf1_s),
    ("PF, combined estimate", big_pf2_s, r_big_pf2_s),
    ("\\textbf{Total}", big_total_s, r_big_total_s),
]
latex_table(
    "lrr",
    ["Stage & Pypomp (1 GPU) & R \\texttt{panelPomp}, 36 cores (estimated) \\\\"],
    [f"{name} & {fmt_dur(g)} & {fmt_dur(r)}" for name, g, r in stages],
)
```

Wall-clock time for fitting the measles model to all towns in England and Wales. Pypomp times were measured on one GPU. R panelPomp times are estimates for a 36-core CPU node, extrapolated from the 4-town panel in @tbl-timing-full$\hspace{0.4mm}.$
